newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW -- Fed leaves funds rate unchanged.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -- Fed leaves funds rate unchanged.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Federal Reserve left the overnight bank lending, or federal funds rate, unchanged.
The rate still stands at 5.50 percent.
U.S. economists were split virtually down the middle over whether the central bank would stand pat on rates or ratchet up the funds rate by 25 basis points.
LYLE GRAMLEY, CONSULTING ECONOMIST, MORTGAGE BANKERS ASSOCIATION, WASHINGTON: "There's very little likelihood of a (rate) move between meetings.

Speaking on Reuters Financial Television, Gramley, a former Federal Reserve Board Governor, continued: "I think we will see further increases in short-term interest rates ... They will continue to be preemptive ... "

KEVIN FLANAGAN, VICE PRESIDENT AND MONEY MARKET ECONOMIST, DEAN WITTER REYNOLDS INC: "It was a close call for the entire Street. The reasoning was we saw some slowing in April. There are no major inflationary expectations."
NEAL SOSS, SENIOR ADVISOR, CREDIT SUISSE FIRST BOSTON:

"What it tells you is that the idea of the Fed forecasting the future and operating on the basis of that forecast has been severely undercut. The absence of any political mandate to act on the basis of their forecast overwhelmed them.

"The Fed has to find a new philosophy for making monetary policy. If the Fed doesn't have confidence in their forecast, how can you use it as a basis of policy? They've apparently given up on the idea that there are inflation risks.

"If they hadn't tightened in March, there would never have been any thought that they would tighten in May, given the news we've gotten," Soss added. "If you believed in March that there are inflation risks inherent in strong growth, then you would still believe that in May. But the news undercut them and undercut their own belief in their own story line -- to the point where they have chosen not to act.
"(Fed Chairman Alan) Greenspan has a story to tell. No one will criticize him for doing nothing. But he still has to articulate a new philosophy for monetary policy," he concluded.
SCOTT PARDEE, SENIOR ADVISOR, YAMAICHI INTERNATIONAL

AMERICA INC: "There is still not enough evidence of inflation. They went 25 basis points (in March) and they still have another 25 or 50 basis points ... but they decided to take a wait-and-see attitude between now and July.

"The economy is slowing down and they want to wait to see how much it is slowing, whether to a 2.0-percent or 3.0-percent growth pattern. They will still have an asymmetric leaning toward tightening, but as long as inflation is not picking up, they have time to wait," Pardee added.

TIM O'NEILL, CHIEF ECONOMIST, HARRIS BANK/BANK OF MONTREAL: "I don't see the likelihood of an inter-meeting move. The rationale for not going today has to have been that they're seeing the expected slowing that Greenspan referred to. You'd have to see a very dramatic shift in the data for May to cause them even to think about an inter-meeting move.
"I thought they were going to go today. It was a very close call, but I thought the necessity for them to go was there in the data, the tightness in the labor market and the product markets.

"The market had already priced out a move, although it was showing some jitteriness about that over the last couple of weeks. There might be a modest rally, but I don't think it will be a sustained one," O'Neill added.

JAMES PADINHA, ECONOMIST, BRIEFING.COM: "For the people looking for a tightening, the first thing that comes to mind is July 2. Most of the tightening forecasts centered on what the Fed was thinking the last time it met. Forecasts a couple of quarters out looked like economic strength combined with some upside inflation risks, and our group didn't feel like those things changed too much between meetings.

"One month of weak April retail sales and one good (Consumer Price Index) number seems like a lot to rest your hat on, so we're going to hold to our view that we still think there's an upside inflation risk (and a bias toward tightening,)" Padinha added.

JOSEPH LIRO, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CIBC WOOD GUNDY SECURITIES CORP: "The market will just focus now on the next economic report that shows a rebound in demand and production ... and build in the expectation that we'll get a move at the July 1-2 meeting instead of today.
Asked about the market reaction to the Fed's decision to leave rates unchanged, Liro said, "Just watch the dollar. The bonds are going to follow the dollar here.
"If the dollar stabilizes you'll get a relief rally, but if it makes new lows, the bond market could not react very positively at all to this news."
JONATHAN BASSILE, ECONOMIST, HSBC MARKETS INC: "It seems that the Fed seems to be happy with the slowdown that's occuring so far in the economy and obviously they're happy with the inflation picture.

"What's next? Well, if they continue to leave rates unchanged then the slowdown has to be through the second quarter ... But honestly, I think the consumer is in good shape and this pull pack in retail spending has probably run its course through April," Bassile added.
CHARLES LIEBERMAN, DIRECTOR OF FINANCIAL MARKETS RESEARCH, CHASE SECURITIES INC: "That's what we were looking for -- no policy announcement, no change in policy and that's it.
"I think the real issue is a question of timing.

"I expected the Fed to leave policy unchanged today but I think rates are going to end up higher and the Fed will end up tightening policy. I didn't expect it today and didn't get it today. Were up 3/8 of a point on the bond. The market shouldn't get too carried away because there is limited upside given the unemployment rate at 4.9 percent and the appearance of a slowdown in economic growth in the second quarter.

"But how much of a slowdown, how sustained that slowdown is, how deep that slowdown is, matters. If the slowdown is 5-1/2 percent to 4.0 percent, then the Fed should have tightened and the markets will regret having rallied. But I think it will take more time to make that judgement," he said.

JOHN LONSKI, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MOODY'S INVESTORS SERVICE INC: "What the Fed did was they heated the slowing of economic activity during April especially that decline by retail sales along with that steep drop in motor vehicle sales, much of the same way they tightened in 1994.
"We have to remember between May of 1994 and August of 1994 ... that's a three-month span that the Fed held policy steady in deference to evidence of a slower economy during that particular episode.

"So, the Fed has held monetary policy steady during previous tightenings and so we should not infer from the unchanged monetary policy following today's meeting that the latest interest rate tightening is already over ... that it has already come to a conclusion.
"I would be (prepared) for a 25-basis-point hike in fed funds in July, with no change in the discount rate," he said.

NICHOLAS PERNA, CHIEF ECONOMIST, FLEET FINANCIAL GROUP: "They didn't do anything...But I'm a firm believer in: 'It ain't over til it's over,' and I think it would be premature to conclude the end of any consideration of upward adjustment of interest rates at their next meeting on July 1 and 2 ... The numbers are what's going to dictate the Fed's actions; the Consumer Price Index, and particularly the unemployment rate." (( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1660 ))
